opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I've become a bit obsessed with lately, because I think it's one of the more underappreciated problems with where language models are heading.

The way we approached it was to start with a large collection of real-world, open-ended queries, the kind people actually ask, like "write a metaphor about time" or "give me ideas for a story." These are questions with no single right answer, where you'd hope for a rich spread of plausible responses. Then we looked at two things. First, intra-model repetition: if you sample the same model many times, even with fairly high temperature, does it keep giving you essentially the same idea? Second, inter-model homogeneity: if you ask many different models, from different companies trained on different data, do they converge on the same answers?

What we found was striking. Both kinds of collapse are real. Models keep repeating themselves, and different models produce remarkably similar outputs, sometimes nearly the same phrasing. For "a metaphor about time," you get "time is a river" and "time is a weaver" over and over, across model families. That's why we call it an "artificial hivemind."

To measure it, we use embedding-based similarity between responses, plus clustering to see how many distinct ideas actually show up. We also collected many human ratings per response, because for open-ended questions people genuinely disagree about what's good. That revealed a second problem: reward models and LLM judges tend to be poorly calibrated when humans have diverse preferences. They assume one correct notion of quality, while real people are pluralistic.

Why does this matter? If billions of people use these systems for brainstorming, writing, and thinking, and every system nudges them toward the same handful of ideas, there's a long-term risk of homogenizing human thought. So I think diversity and pluralism need to be first-class evaluation targets, not an afterthought behind accuracy or helpfulness.

r001.rationale: It says repeated samples from the same model can keep giving essentially the same idea, even at fairly high temperature.

r002.rationale: It says different models converge on remarkably similar answers, sometimes nearly identical in phrasing.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've been thinking about a lot, because I think diversity is one of the most underappreciated dimensions when we evaluate these models. We're very good at measuring whether a response is correct, or whether a human prefers it over another one, but we rarely ask: if you ask the model the same open-ended question many times, or across many users, how different are the answers actually?

So the first thing we do is just sample a lot. You take a question that genuinely admits many valid answers, something like "write a short story about a dog" or "what's a good gift for a friend," and you sample dozens or hundreds of responses. Then you look at the distribution, not individual outputs.

And there are different levels at which you can measure diversity. The most superficial is lexical, so things like distinct n-grams, self-BLEU, how much the responses repeat each other at the surface. That's cheap and easy, but it's also easy to fool. A model can vary the wording while saying essentially the same thing.

So the more interesting level is semantic diversity. Here we'll embed the responses, or we'll have another model cluster them, and ask: how many genuinely distinct ideas or approaches are in this set? If I ask for a story and I get two hundred stories, and a hundred and ninety of them are about a golden retriever named Max who gets lost and finds his way home, that's a very collapsed distribution, even if every sentence is phrased differently.

And then there's an even higher level, which I'd call perspective or stance diversity. For questions that touch on values or where reasonable people disagree, does the model always converge on the same framing, the same "safe" middle position, the same structure of "on one hand, on the other hand"? We've found that post-training, especially RLHF, tends to really sharpen the distribution. The base model might actually have a broader range, and the alignment process narrows it toward whatever the reward model found most agreeable.

The other thing I always want to pair diversity with is quality, because it's trivially easy to get diversity by being random. So we'll typically look at a quality-diversity trade-off curve rather than a single number. And ideally you compare against the human distribution. If you ask a hundred people the same open-ended question, how spread out are their answers? That's the reference point, and what we often see is that models are much more concentrated than people are, which has real consequences if everyone is using the same few systems to write and think.

r001.rationale: The response describes homogeneous semantic outputs across many samples, but does not mention higher-temperature sampling.

r002.rationale: The response discusses a model’s output distribution and compares models with people, but does not state that different language models behave similarly.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is, diversity across what? You can ask an open-ended question and get responses that use different words, but essentially express the same idea. So variation in wording alone doesn’t tell us very much. We want to understand whether the model offers genuinely different perspectives, assumptions, or approaches.

And then there’s the question of whose perspectives are represented. An open-ended question may have many reasonable answers depending on someone’s cultural background or values. A model can sound very balanced while repeatedly favoring a narrow set of viewpoints. So I would look at repeated responses to the same question, as well as responses to different phrasings, and assess the range of meanings—not just the range of words. Human judgment matters here, because diversity is useful only if those different answers are also relevant and coherent.

r001.rationale: It recommends examining repeated responses, but does not say they may remain homogeneous when sampled at higher temperature.

r002.rationale: It does not compare different language models or state that their open-ended answers show similar behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish between diversity in wording and diversity in ideas. You can ask a model the same open-ended question multiple times and get responses that look different, but they may all be expressing essentially the same perspective.

So I would look at the range of viewpoints, assumptions, and possible solutions those responses represent. And then I would compare that with responses from people with different backgrounds. Are there perspectives that people bring up that the model consistently misses? Does the model gravitate toward one conventional answer, even when many reasonable answers exist?

The challenge is that diversity alone isn’t enough. Random or incoherent answers can be very different from each other. What we really want is a variety of meaningful, relevant answers, without treating the most common perspective as the only valid one.

r001.rationale: The response says repeated answers may differ in wording while expressing the same perspective, but it does not mention higher-temperature sampling.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare behavior across different language models.
